overview:
Mangal-divo (also spelled Mangal Deevo or Mangal Divo) is a devotional lamp ritual found primarily in Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka Jain practice, usually performed together with ārati at the conclusion of pūjā or other temple worship. The term combines "mangal" (auspicious, purifying, conducive to spiritual welfare) and "dīvo" (lamp), so the central idea is an "auspicious lamp" that symbolizes inner illumination rather than a material offering demanded by the Jina.

Historically, the custom of ārati and Mangal-divo appears to have developed in the medieval period, around the 12th century CE, in western India. Traditional narratives connect its spread to the influence of Ācārya Hemacandra and the Jain lay king Kumārapāla of Gujarat, who promoted non-violence and Jain dharma in a context where many Jains were drifting toward other religious practices. In this setting, the use of lamps and devotional songs at the end of worship became a way to express intense bhakti while still affirming core Jain principles such as ahiṃsā and the non-possessive, desireless nature of the Tīrthaṅkaras.

In ritual practice, Mangal-divo is usually performed after the eightfold worship (aṣṭaprakārī pūjā) and ārati. Several lamps—often five—are lit to represent the Pañca-Parameṣṭhī (Arihant, Siddha, Ācārya, Upādhyāya, and Sādhu). The flame is gently circled before the Jina image while a specific Mangal-divo hymn is sung. The lamp’s light is interpreted as the radiance of right knowledge and right faith, dispelling the darkness of delusion (moha) and karmic ignorance. The Jina, being vītarāga and completely fulfilled, does not need light or offerings; instead, the devotee uses the symbol of light to cultivate inner purity, gratitude, and resolve to follow the path of liberation.

Theologically, Mangal-divo is understood as a meditative and emotional culmination of worship. The lamp stands for the five kinds of knowledge and the awakening of the soul, while the term "mangal" is explained as that which filters or purifies the self from inauspicious states. Community explanations emphasize that ārati and Mangal-divo are for the spiritual joy and concentration of the worshipper, not for changing the state of the liberated beings. In many contemporary Jain communities, especially in Gujarat and diaspora temples, Mangal-divo remains a cherished part of daily or festival worship, linking doctrinally careful Jain philosophy with a warm, participatory devotional atmosphere.

Across traditions, there is some variation: Digambara communities may have different lamp customs or emphasize other concluding hymns, and some Sthānakavāsī and non-image-worshipping groups minimize or avoid lamp rituals altogether, focusing instead on scriptural recitation and meditation. Even within Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka practice, the exact wording, melody, and performance style of the Mangal-divo hymn can differ by region and temple. Yet the shared core remains the same: the lamp is a reminder that true auspiciousness lies in purifying one’s own inner states through refuge in the Arihants, Siddhas, sādhus, and the dharma they reveal.

primary_sources.title: Traditional explanation of ārati and Mangal-deevo
primary_sources.author: Attributed to community teachers drawing on Hemacandra and Kumārapāla narratives
primary_sources.original_text: आरती और मंगल दीपक जैन पूजा का समापन होता है आरती और मंगल दीवो से — वह क्षण जब प्रकाश की लौ परमात्मा के सामने झुकती है। जैन दर्शन में परमात्मा वीतरागी हैं — उन्हें किसी वस्तु की आवश्यकता नहीं। फिर भी आरती क्यों? क्योंकि आरती परमात्मा के लिए नहीं — साधक की भाव-शुद्धि के लिए है।
primary_sources.transliteration: Āratī aur mangal dīpak Jain pūjā kā samāpan hotā hai ārati aur mangal dīvo se — vah kṣaṇ jab prakāś kī lau paramātmā ke sāmne jhuktī hai. Jain darśan meṃ paramātmā vītarāgī haiṃ — unheṃ kisī vastu kī āvaśyaktā nahīṃ. Phir bhī ārati kyoṃ? Kyoṃki ārati paramātmā ke liye nahīṃ — sādhak kī bhāva-śuddhi ke liye hai.
primary_sources.translation: In Jain worship, ārati and Mangal-divo mark the conclusion of pūjā—the moment when the flame of light bows before the Supreme Being. In Jain philosophy, the Supreme is vītarāga, free from all passions, and needs nothing. Why then ārati? Because ārati is not for the Supreme Being; it is for the purification of the devotee’s inner feelings.
primary_sources.notes: This passage represents a widely taught doctrinal framing in modern Jain educational literature: the lamp is explicitly said to be for the worshipper’s bhāva-śuddhi (purification of attitude), not for fulfilling any need of the Jina. It reflects Tier D community education that aligns with classical doctrine about vītarāga Tīrthaṅkaras.

primary_sources.title: Background of ārati and Mangal-deevo
primary_sources.author: Modern educational summary based on Hemacandra–Kumārapāla tradition
primary_sources.original_text: The practice of ärati and mangaldeevo was started around 12th Century AD (almost 900 years ago) by the inspiration of Acharya Hemchandraji. It was a time when a lot of Jains were getting converted into other religions such as Hinduism and the practice of animal slaughter that Mahavir Swami had stopped during his times was getting popular again. Acharya Hemchandraji inspired the then Hindu King Kumarpal of Gujarat with his teaching of non-violence and explaining the true meaning of religion. King Kumarpal became a Jain shäravak and is said to have started the practice of Ärati and Deevo and declared the state of Gujarat as a non-violent state.
primary_sources.transliteration: The practice of ārati and mangal-dīvo was started around 12th Century AD by the inspiration of Ācārya Hemacandrajī… King Kumārapāl became a Jain śrāvaka and is said to have started the practice of ārati and dīvo and declared the state of Gujarat as a non-violent state.
primary_sources.translation: The practice of ārati and Mangal-deevo is said to have begun around the 12th century CE, inspired by Ācārya Hemacandra. At that time many Jains were converting to other religions and animal slaughter, which Mahāvīra had stopped, was becoming common again. Ācārya Hemacandra inspired the Hindu king Kumārapāla of Gujarat with teachings of non-violence and the true meaning of religion. King Kumārapāla became a Jain lay follower and is said to have started the practice of ārati and the lamp (deevo), declaring Gujarat a non-violent state.
primary_sources.notes: This is a historical-traditional account found in community booklets and lectures. It is not a direct quotation from Hemacandra’s Sanskrit works but a later narrative (Tier D–C) that situates ārati and Mangal-divo in the Hemacandra–Kumārapāla milieu. Scholars treat it as a devotional-historical tradition rather than a verifiable primary source.

primary_sources.title: Jain ārati attributed to Śeth Mulchand of Dhudeva (Kesaryaji)
primary_sources.author: Śeth Mulchand (traditional attribution)
primary_sources.original_text:
जय जय आरती आदि जिनन्दा, नाभिराया मरुदेवी को नन्दा…
पंचमी आरती पुण्य उपाय्या, मुलचंदे ऋषभ गुण गाया…
primary_sources.transliteration:
Jaya jaya ārati ādi jinandā, nābhirāyā Marudevī ko nandā…
Pañcamī ārati puṇya upāyā, Mulchande ṛṣabh guṇa gāyā…
primary_sources.translation: Victory, victory to the ārati of the primordial Jina, beloved son of King Nābhi and Queen Marudevī… With the fifth ārati, according to Śeth Mulchand, by singing the virtues of Ṛṣabhadeva, the worshipper gains merit (puṇya).
primary_sources.notes: This ārati, sung immediately before or together with Mangal-divo in many Śvetāmbara temples, is traditionally attributed to Śeth Mulchand of Dhudeva–Kesaryaji in Rajasthan. Only brief lines are quoted here to avoid reproducing the full copyrighted hymn. The text is late-medieval vernacular rather than canonical Prakrit or Sanskrit, and functions as a bhakti composition praising Ādinātha/Ṛṣabhadeva.

primary_sources.title: Conceptual definition of Mangal-divo in modern Jain teaching
primary_sources.author: Contemporary Jain educational sources
primary_sources.original_text: Mangal Divo (auspicious lamp): A lamp lit at the start of prayer or ritual to invite auspiciousness, dispel darkness, and remind devotees to seek spiritual illumination. It is placed before Tirthankaras or in the prayer space as a sign of reverence and to create a sacred atmosphere.
primary_sources.transliteration: Mangal Divo (auspicious lamp): A lamp lit at the start of prayer or ritual to invite auspiciousness, dispel darkness, and remind devotees to seek spiritual illumination.
primary_sources.translation: Mangal-divo (auspicious lamp) is described as a lamp lit at the beginning of prayer or ritual to invite auspiciousness, dispel darkness, and remind devotees to seek spiritual illumination. It is placed before the Tīrthaṅkaras or in the prayer space as a sign of reverence and to create a sacred atmosphere.
primary_sources.notes: This is a concise conceptual definition from recent Jain educational materials (Tier D), summarizing the symbolic meaning of the lamp in line with classical doctrine about light as a metaphor for knowledge and spiritual clarity.

misconceptions.myth: Mangal-divo is a material offering that the Jina or liberated beings need in order to be pleased or to grant worldly favors.
misconceptions.reality: Jain doctrine emphasizes that Arihants and Siddhas are vītarāga—completely free from desire, attachment, and need. The lamp is not for them but for the worshipper’s own inner purification and concentration. Mangal-divo symbolizes the light of right knowledge dispelling ignorance; it does not change the state of the liberated beings or compel them to grant boons.

misconceptions.myth: Mangal-divo is simply a borrowed Hindu ritual and therefore not truly Jain or philosophically consistent with Jain teachings.
misconceptions.reality: While lamp worship is widespread in South Asian religions, Jain communities have given Mangal-divo a distinctly Jain interpretation rooted in ahiṃsā, vītarāgatā, and the symbolism of knowledge. Traditional narratives link its development to Hemacandra and Kumārapāla, and modern explanations stress that the lamp is a reminder of the Pañca-Parameṣṭhī and the path of liberation, not a sacrifice or propitiatory offering. Its meaning is carefully aligned with Jain philosophy even if the outward form resembles other regional practices.

misconceptions.myth: Skipping Mangal-divo or ārati after pūjā is a grave sin that automatically leads to bad rebirth or heavy karmic bondage.
misconceptions.reality: In Jain karma theory, bondage depends on the intensity of passions (kaṣāya) and the quality of one’s inner states, not on mechanical performance of specific rituals. Mangal-divo is a recommended devotional practice that can support right faith and concentration, but its omission is not in itself a catastrophic sin. What matters more is whether one cultivates non-violence, self-restraint, and sincere effort toward right view, knowledge, and conduct.

misconceptions.myth: The physical flame of Mangal-divo directly burns away karmas or removes all obstacles in a magical, automatic way.
misconceptions.reality: Jain teaching treats the lamp as a symbol: the "burning" of darkness represents the gradual removal of ignorance and delusion through right effort, study, and meditation. Karmas are shed by disciplined practice of vows, meditation, and reduction of passions, not by the physical properties of fire. Mangal-divo can inspire and focus the mind, but it is the inner transformation—guided by the refuges of Arihant, Siddha, sādhus, and dharma—that actually reduces karmic bondage.

misconceptions.myth: All Jain traditions must perform Mangal-divo in the same way, and any variation or non-use is a deviation from authentic Jainism.
misconceptions.reality: Jain traditions are diverse. Śvetāmbara Mūrtipūjaka communities commonly perform ārati and Mangal-divo, while some Sthānakavāsī and non-image-worshipping groups emphasize scriptural recitation and meditation without lamps. Digambara communities may have different concluding hymns or lamp customs. Authenticity is measured by adherence to core Jain principles—ahiṃsā, anekāntavāda, and the path of liberation—rather than uniformity in one particular ritual form.
